title: SGLang 101
subtitle: Serving language models with SGLang, from one request to a fleet, with the judgment the flag list leaves out
summary: How SGLang turns GPU memory and time into tokens, why each feature exists, and which defaults to trust. Local listings come from recorded runs of SGLang 0.5.22.
audience: You are an engineer who has called a model API and wants to serve an open model yourself. You know what a token and a GPU are. You have not read a serving engine's scheduler or cache, and you want to know which settings matter before you pay for them.
outcomes: Start SGLang, send a request, and read every line the scheduler logs about it.
Compute the KV cache cost of a model, size the pool on purpose, and explain why a server runs out of memory.
Write prompts that hit the prefix cache, and prove the hit rate with cached_tokens and /metrics.
Benchmark a server, find the concurrency knee, and report TTFT, TPOT, and throughput together.
Choose between tensor, data, and expert parallelism and prefill-decode disaggregation from measurements.
Judge a published SGLang benchmark: its version, its workload, and the mechanism that explains its result.

plate.title: One request, three processes, one cache
plate.caption: A chat request from our capture crosses the three processes. The radix cache served 2,998 of its 2,999 prompt tokens. From capture/out/cache-experiment.txt.

parts.title: SGLang on One Page
parts.thesis: A serving engine exists to keep an expensive GPU busy on tokens nobody computed before, and every SGLang feature serves that goal.
parts.summary: Prefill against decode, the four numbers every server is judged by, and one complete request from our capture.

parts.title: The Request Path
parts.thesis: A request crosses three processes, and the scheduler between them decides who runs, who waits, and who gets thrown out.
parts.summary: sglang serve, the scheduler loop and its policies, admission and retraction, the overlap scheduler, and the response path.

parts.title: The KV Cache
parts.thesis: Memory, not compute, decides how many users one GPU can serve, and the radix tree decides how much of that memory you pay for twice.
parts.summary: Bytes per token, startup sizing, RadixCache, prefix-friendly prompts, eviction and HiCache, and hybrid models.

parts.title: Each Forward Pass
parts.thesis: Most decode time is launch overhead and memory traffic, so SGLang picks graphs, kernels, and draft tokens for your GPU before you ask.
parts.summary: ForwardMode and CUDA graphs, attention backends, quantization, speculative decoding, structured outputs, and deterministic inference.

parts.title: Measuring a Server
parts.thesis: A throughput number without a latency target describes nothing, so measure the knee before you tune anything.
parts.summary: sglang.benchmark.serving, the /metrics endpoint, and how to read benchmarks that other people publish.

parts.title: One Server Becomes a Fleet
parts.thesis: Split a model across GPUs only after one GPU is saturated, and split prefill from decode only after you measured that prefill hurts.
parts.summary: Tensor, data, attention-data, and expert parallelism, MoE serving, prefill-decode disaggregation, and the model gateway.

parts.title: Production and Training
parts.thesis: Operate SGLang with its defaults written down, and expect reinforcement learning to treat the server as part of the training loop.
parts.summary: Deploying and tuning in order, and SGLang as the rollout engine of Miles.
